edition.editorialNote: Grouped reports about the same event where they add useful context or distinct evidence. Allegations and forecasts are attributed, and unresolved matters are kept explicit.

content.headline: Russian strikes hit Kyiv bridge as Merz visits with new air-defence support
content.shortHeadline: Kyiv bridge hit as Merz pledges new support
content.standfirst: A Russian drone strike damaged a key crossing over the Dnipro for a fourth day of attacks on Kyiv’s bridges, disrupting journeys across the city. Germany announced support including joint production of interceptor drones.

image.caption: Soldiers inspect damage to Kyiv’s Northern Bridge after a Russian drone strike.

sources.originalTitle: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support
Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
Putins nye doktrin varsler hårde tider for Ukraine

segments.body: A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on Sunday, injuring two people, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The attack was the latest in four consecutive days of strikes on bridges across the Dnipro, which connect the city’s eastern and western banks. The crossings remain standing, but restrictions have caused traffic disruption.

segments.title: Support as attacks intensify
segments.body: The strike came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made an unannounced visit to Kyiv. Germany said it would fund joint production of drones designed to intercept Russian jet-powered drones; Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, also said a new aid package had been agreed. Air-raid sirens sounded during the visit.

perspectives.body: TV 2 reports Zelenskyy’s allegation that a new Russian military directive permits attacks on a wider range of civilian targets. The report says the claim has not been independently verified; the Kremlin has denied targeting civilians.

content.headline: Brazil votes in tight Lula–Bolsonaro race amid corruption allegations
content.shortHeadline: Brazil votes in close Lula–Bolsonaro contest
content.standfirst: Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro are the only presidential contenders polling near 40%, with a run-off expected if neither wins more than half the valid votes. Allegations linked to a jailed banker have also become a campaign issue.

image.caption: Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro are the two leading candidates in Brazil’s presidential race.

sources.originalTitle: What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
Skandalernes tid: Brasilien går til valg med sex-skandale som bagtæppe

segments.body: Brazilians are voting in a presidential election that pits incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Polls cited by the BBC put both leading candidates around 40%, with Lula slightly ahead; a second round is scheduled for 25 October if no candidate wins a majority.

segments.title: Scandals shadow the campaign
segments.body: A jailed banker, Daniel Vorcaro, has become a focus of competing corruption allegations. Flávio Bolsonaro acknowledged asking Vorcaro to finance a film about his father, and police have opened an investigation into suspected corruption and money laundering. Lula ally and Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes has denied wrongdoing after investigators said Vorcaro contacted a number linked to him.

perspectives.body: DR’s South America correspondent describes the Vorcaro affair as reaching figures on both sides of Brazil’s political divide, while judging that current scrutiny may be more damaging to Flávio Bolsonaro. The report also highlights an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro endorsing his son.

content.headline: Yemen government declares war to retake Houthi-held territory
content.shortHeadline: Yemen government vows all-out war on Houthis
content.standfirst: President Rashad al-Alimi announced military operations to reclaim territory as the Houthis and Saudi-led forces exchange strikes. The group says it attacked Saudi oil sites, but Saudi Arabia has not commented on that claim.

image.caption: Soldiers travel near Taiz, where fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis continues.

sources.originalTitle: Yemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from Houthis

segments.body: Yemen’s internationally recognised president, Rashad al-Alimi, says his government is beginning military operations to retake territory held by the Houthis. The announcement follows renewed fighting and comes as the Houthis claim to have struck Saudi Aramco sites; Saudi Arabia has not commented on that claim.

segments.title: A widening conflict
segments.body: The Houthis have made recent gains, including cutting a supply route linking the government-held city of Taiz with Aden, the interim capital, according to AFP reporting cited by the BBC. The conflict, which began in 2014 and has caused a major humanitarian crisis, has reignited amid wider regional fighting.

content.headline: Ethiopian rebels leave Mekelle as fighting moves towards Tigray capital
content.shortHeadline: TPLF withdraws from Tigray capital as fighting nears
content.standfirst: The Tigray People’s Liberation Front says it has temporarily withdrawn from Mekelle to reduce risks to civilians. Residents told the BBC pro-government forces now control the city as renewed conflict raises fears of wider regional instability.

image.caption: A pro-government soldier stands guard in Tigray as fighting resumes in the region.

sources.originalTitle: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital

segments.body: The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) says it has temporarily withdrawn from Mekelle, the regional capital, as fighting with Ethiopian federal forces approaches. The group said the move was intended to address risks to civilians. Two residents told the BBC that pro-government forces had taken control of the city.

segments.title: Fears of a wider crisis
segments.body: The renewed fighting follows months of worsening relations and mutual accusations of violating the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. Ethiopia and Eritrea have also severed diplomatic relations, while the United Nations says insecurity in northern Ethiopia is disrupting humanitarian work and calls for safe access to people in need.

content.headline: Spain’s housing protests grow after emergency rent measures fail
content.shortHeadline: Spain protests follow defeat of emergency housing measures
content.standfirst: Thousands marched after parliament rejected measures including eviction protections and rental extensions. The vote leaves Pedro Sánchez’s minority government under pressure as housing costs and shortages continue to fuel public anger.

image.caption: Demonstrators protest in Spain over the housing crisis and the cost of renting.

sources.originalTitle: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis

segments.body: Thousands of people took part in about 50 protests across Spain on Saturday, calling for stronger tenant protections after parliament rejected emergency housing measures. The proposals included suspending some evictions, extending rental leases and restricting purchases by investment funds.

segments.title: A deepening housing crunch
segments.body: The demonstrations follow the eviction of an 87-year-old woman after a sharp rent rise. The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes; national figures show house prices rose 12.2% in the year to the second quarter of 2026. In Valencia, police and demonstrators clashed, and nine officers were reported injured.

content.headline: Indian journalists allege sexual harassment during voter-roll protests
content.shortHeadline: Journalists allege harassment as India voter-roll protests grow
content.standfirst: Three female journalists say police sexually harassed them during protests demanding the election chief’s resignation. Police say the complaint has been referred to the crime branch as demonstrations continue over a revision that has removed 130 million names from voter rolls.

image.caption: Young people protest changes to India’s voter rolls.

sources.originalTitle: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest

segments.body: Three female journalists have accused police officers of sexual harassment during protests in Delhi. Delhi Police said it had received the complaint and transferred it to its crime branch for an inquiry. Police also detained dozens of demonstrators calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign.

segments.title: Dispute over voter lists
segments.body: Protests in Delhi and Mumbai continued for a third day over changes to voter rolls that have removed 130 million names so far. The Election Commission says the revision removes duplicate and ineligible entries; opposition parties accuse it of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP, an allegation both the commission and BJP reject.

content.headline: Australia investigates Flydubai co-pilot’s links after cockpit attack
content.shortHeadline: Australia probes co-pilot’s links after flight attack
content.standfirst: Australian authorities are examining the co-pilot’s ties to the country after he allegedly attacked the captain with a crash axe on a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight. Passengers helped regain control, and the plane landed safely in Saudi Arabia.

image.caption: The Flydubai aircraft was diverted after passengers helped the crew regain control.

sources.originalTitle: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country

segments.body: Australian police and security agencies are investigating a Flydubai co-pilot’s links to Australia after an alleged attack on the captain during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The plane descended sharply before passengers helped the crew regain control and two reserve pilots landed it safely in Saudi Arabia.

segments.title: Investigation ongoing
segments.body: The UAE prosecutor says the incident is being investigated as an attempted terrorist act and is examining possible motives and links. Australian media report the co-pilot studied in Australia from 2015 to 2017; those reports also say his student visa was cancelled in 2019. Authorities have not publicly identified him.

content.headline: Police data show thousands of sexual offences against children at schools
content.shortHeadline: Police record thousands of sexual offences against children at schools
content.standfirst: A Guardian analysis of data from 33 forces found at least 8,500 reported sexual offences against children aged 12 and under at or near schools in England and Wales from 2021 to 2025. The true scale is uncertain and may be higher.

sources.originalTitle: Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales
From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schools

segments.body: Police recorded at least 8,500 sexual offences against children aged 12 and under as occurring on or near school premises in England and Wales between 2021 and 2025, according to the Guardian’s analysis of freedom of information data. The figures include nearly 2,000 reports of rape or attempted rape.

segments.title: Reporting and response
segments.body: The analysis covers responses from 33 of 43 police forces, and the Guardian says the total is likely to be higher. Many records do not specify the alleged perpetrator’s age. The children’s commissioner for England called peer-on-peer abuse widespread and too often brushed aside; a police lead said greater awareness may also be increasing reporting.

segments.title: What happens after a report
segments.body: Lawyers and campaigners interviewed by the Guardian say some schools struggle to protect pupils and support victims during investigations. One lawyer described cases where children continued at the same school without adequate safety measures; the report also notes that incidents can go unreported and that schools face complex safeguarding responsibilities.

content.headline: Green Party adopts divisive motion equating Zionism with racism
content.shortHeadline: Greens adopt divisive motion on Zionism and racism
content.standfirst: Members voted 1,022 to 813 for a policy motion defining Zionism as racism and backing a single Palestinian state. Most Green MPs opposed it, while Jewish members and organisations raised concerns about discrimination and how the policy may be applied.

image.caption: Israeli flags outside the Green Party conference venue in Brighton.

sources.originalTitle: Green party votes to adopt policy that equates Zionism with racism
Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' motion
Green Party passes ‘Zionism is racism’ motion – but Polanski misses vote

segments.body: The Green Party of England and Wales has adopted a binding policy motion describing Zionism as a form of racism and supporting a single democratic Palestinian state. The vote at the party’s Brighton conference was 1,022 to 813. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion; leader Zack Polanski did not vote.

segments.title: Divisions and safeguards
segments.body: Polanski said he wanted the text amended, including to protect Jewish members who attend synagogues that identify as Zionist, but members rejected his proposed changes. The party says it will protect Jewish members from discrimination. Some Jewish Greens have expressed concern about their future in the party.

segments.title: Possible legal challenge
segments.body: Jewish organisations criticised the motion, while a barrister cited by the Guardian said it risked breaching the Equality Act. That is a legal assessment, not a court ruling: the Guardian reports that some Green members are consulting lawyers about a possible challenge.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that some members are considering an Equality Act challenge and quotes barrister Adam Wagner KC, who says the policy may discriminate against or harass Jewish people and people holding Zionist beliefs.

content.headline: Badenoch sets out smaller-state Conservative agenda as conference opens
content.shortHeadline: Badenoch sets out Conservative plans for cuts and growth
content.standfirst: At the party conference, Kemi Badenoch argued for tax cuts, deregulation and a smaller state, while unveiling proposals on childcare and prison places. A leaked account suggests the party has discussed savings beyond the £47bn already outlined.

image.caption: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch at the party conference in Birmingham.

sources.originalTitle: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals
Tories would expand free childcare to high earners, Badenoch says
Return of the nasty party? Badenoch walks tightrope with ‘punch down’ policies

segments.body: Kemi Badenoch opened the Conservatives’ Birmingham conference by calling herself a “classic old school Conservative” and arguing that business, not government, creates growth. Her published essay proposes tax cuts, deregulation and reducing the civil service to pre-pandemic levels.

segments.title: Proposals and their trade-offs
segments.body: The party has proposed extending free childcare in England to working parents earning above the current £100,000 threshold, at an estimated annual cost of £700m, and creating 50,000 prison places partly by cutting overseas aid. Badenoch says the party would also make further spending savings; a leaked account from shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said ministers had discussed cuts across government.

segments.title: Questions about political appeal
segments.body: Badenoch is seeking to distinguish the party from Labour and Reform UK as the Conservatives remain behind them in polls. A Guardian report describes concern among some Conservatives that the party’s emphasis on restrictive social policies could alienate moderate voters, despite a more positive mood at the conference.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account highlights internal unease that the party’s focus on winning back Reform voters risks narrowing its appeal. A shadow minister warns that some policies could revive the Conservatives’ reputation as the “nasty party”.

content.headline: Farage questioned over whether he should have declared £5m gift
content.shortHeadline: Farage interviewed over £5m gift declaration
content.standfirst: The Reform UK leader was interviewed by Parliament’s standards commissioner as part of an inquiry into a £5m gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Farage says it was for personal security and did not need to be registered.

image.caption: Nigel Farage says the £5m gift was for his personal security.

sources.originalTitle: Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift
Green Party passes ‘Zionism is racism’ motion – but Polanski misses vote

segments.body: Nigel Farage was interviewed for about half an hour last month by the parliamentary standards commissioner, the Sunday Times reported. The inquiry concerns whether he should have declared a £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, a crypto billionaire. Farage says the money was for his personal security, not political activity.

segments.title: Possible next steps
segments.body: The inquiry has not concluded. If the commissioner finds a serious breach, the matter could go to the Commons standards committee, which can recommend a sanction. A suspension of more than 10 sitting days, if approved by Parliament, could trigger a recall petition in Farage’s Clacton constituency.

content.headline: Justice secretary cannot say how many early-release prisoners are tagged
content.shortHeadline: Ministers cannot yet say how many early-release prisoners are tagged
content.standfirst: Alex Norris said it was too soon to give figures after about 700 men were released early from prisons in England and Wales. The government says electronic tagging is presumed, but released prisoners told the Guardian they had not been fitted with tags.

image.caption: Justice Secretary Alex Norris said it was too soon to give figures on tagging.

sources.originalTitle: UK justice secretary unable to say how many early release prisoners have been tagged

segments.body: Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he could not yet say how many of roughly 700 men released early on Thursday had been fitted with electronic tags. The government introduced a presumption of tagging to manage prison overcrowding; nearly 5,000 prisoners are due to be released in stages over the next year.

segments.title: Concerns about monitoring
segments.body: Several prisoners told the Guardian they had not been tagged, and one said he did not know when that would happen. The report also notes that a probation inspectorate recently found delays of up to five months in fitting tags, raising concerns about monitoring and victim safety.

content.headline: Reported assaults on Britain’s railways reach record as staff and passengers say
content.shortHeadline: Rail assaults reach record as staff and passengers report abuse
content.standfirst: Reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways rose by a fifth to nearly 25,000 in 2025–26, including almost 2,500 physical assaults on workers. Unions cite falling transport-police numbers, while police say increased reporting explains part of the rise.

image.caption: Rail staff use body-worn cameras to record incidents of violence and abuse.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The violence is off the scale’: staff and passengers at risk as assaults on trains in Great Britain soar to record high

segments.body: Reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways reached nearly 25,000 in 2025–26, a fifth higher than the previous year, according to figures from the Office of Rail and Road. The total includes threats and verbal abuse as well as physical contact; nearly 2,500 reports involved physical assaults on rail workers.

segments.title: Safety and reporting
segments.body: Rail workers describe threats and assaults, while passengers recount sexual harassment and homophobic abuse. Unions are calling for more staffed stations and police, noting that British Transport Police numbers fell by more than 10% between 2024 and 2026. Police say more discreet reporting methods have contributed to the increase in reported passenger assaults.

segments.title: Response
segments.body: The Department for Transport calls the rise deeply concerning and says it has committed £63m in additional British Transport Police funding by 2028–29, supporting more than 200 additional officers and investment in CCTV and body-worn video. Police advise passengers to text 61016 or call 999 in an emergency.

content.headline: Social landlords with repeated failings receive grants to build new homes
content.shortHeadline: Housing providers with poor repair records receive building grants
content.standfirst: An investigation found six housing associations receiving government grants for new homes each had more than 100 maladministration findings last year. Providers cite improvements and investment; the ombudsman says severe findings have fallen overall.

image.caption: The investigation documents reports of mould and pest problems in social housing.

sources.originalTitle: Landlords of damp, mice-infested houses are building Burnham’s new homes

segments.body: Six housing associations selected for government funding to build affordable homes each received more than 100 Housing Ombudsman findings of maladministration in the past year, an i Paper investigation found. The programme distributes £9.5bn among 33 providers as the government seeks to expand social and affordable housing.

segments.title: Conditions and accountability
segments.body: Reported cases include delays to repairs, damp and mould, and pest infestations. The report gives examples involving Clarion, Sanctuary and other landlords, alongside their responses: providers say they have taken steps to improve services, resolve complaints and invest in existing homes. The ombudsman says severe maladministration findings fell in 2025–26.

segments.title: Pressure to build and repair
segments.body: Experts quoted in the investigation argue that grant decisions should take account of tenants’ living conditions and regulatory performance. The National Housing Federation says associations spent a record £9.7bn on repairs and maintenance last year, while also facing pressure to build homes amid a shortage of social housing.

content.headline: Police admit they should have updated caller before woman was found dead
content.shortHeadline: Police admit they should have called back after emergency report
content.standfirst: A neighbour twice reported worrying sounds from a 23-year-old woman’s flat in Odense, but police did not attend or tell him they had changed their response. Fyn Police say its call-centre procedures have since been tightened.

sources.originalTitle: Nabo ringede forgæves: Politiet erkender fejl i sag om 23-årigs død

segments.body: Fyn Police say they should have told a caller they would not attend after he reported unusual sounds from his upstairs neighbour’s flat in the early hours of 4 August last year. The 23-year-old, Cecilie Voller Kjærulff, was found dead the next day.

segments.title: What is known—and disputed
segments.body: An autopsy concluded she likely died from an overdose of medication prescribed for bipolar disorder; traces of MDMA, cocaine and alcohol were also found. Experts who spoke to DR said she would likely have survived if she had reached hospital when the neighbour called. Police say that, based on what dispatchers knew at the time, the call did not appear to require an urgent response.

segments.title: Procedures changed
segments.body: The police inspector says the force has tightened call-centre procedures, including requiring staff to use a specific questioning technique and to tell callers when a promised response will not happen. Kjærulff’s parents remain strongly critical and say the changes offer little comfort.

content.headline: Neighbours fear losses as planned ammunition factory advances in northern Jut J
content.shortHeadline: Neighbours fear homes will lose value near planned ammunition factory
content.standfirst: Residents near a planned factory in Elling say estate agents warn their homes may be difficult to sell and are asking for compensation or buyouts. The defence minister says he is willing to consider compensation if residents suffer significant or lasting problems.

image.caption: Leif Boie Thomsen lives near the planned ammunition factory in Elling.

sources.originalTitle: Risikerer milliontab: Nabo til krudtfabrik rystet

segments.body: Residents living in a proposed safety zone around the Krudten ammunition factory in Elling, northern Jutland, say they fear being unable to sell their homes. One neighbour, Leif Boie Thomsen, says estate agents have suggested a sale could require a price reduction of more than one million kroner.

segments.title: Compensation still uncertain
segments.body: Residents say they are worried about living beside a large factory and frustrated that they have not received clear information about compensation or property buyouts. Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus says he understands their concerns and would consider compensation if the factory causes residents significant or lasting problems. Thomsen questions whether the risk to property values would qualify.

content.headline: North Jutland ambulance call-outs rise as staff question dispatches
content.shortHeadline: North Jutland ambulance call-outs rise 29% in five years
content.standfirst: The region recorded 32% more 112 calls in 2025 than in 2020 and a 29% rise in ambulance journeys for urgent and serious cases. A staff representative says some dispatches could be avoided; regional management defends the call-centre assessments.

sources.originalTitle: Ambulanceture er eksploderet – giver store problemer

segments.body: North Jutland recorded 32% more emergency calls in 2025 than in 2020, while ambulance journeys for acute or serious cases rose 29%, to 38,586, regional figures show. An ambulance staff representative says the increase is putting pressure on crews and may leave fewer vehicles available for urgent incidents.

segments.title: Dispute over dispatch decisions
segments.body: Lars Jakobsen, a staff representative in Hjørring, says crews are sometimes sent to cases he believes could be handled by relatives or other health services. Martin Rostgaard-Knudsen, the region’s medical director, says dispatchers assess calls carefully and may send an ambulance to establish what help a patient needs.

content.headline: Danish investment fund denies allegations in US concert-business lawsuit
content.shortHeadline: Waterland denies allegations in US Christian music lawsuit
content.standfirst: A US company alleges Waterland and two Danish employees used confidential information to build a competing sponsorship business and tried to damage its reputation. Waterland denies the claims and is asking a Tennessee judge to dismiss the case.

sources.originalTitle: Interne mails, kristen musik og voldtægtsbeskyldninger: Dansk kapitalfond beskyldes for at ville 'knuse' konkurrent

segments.body: A US company, Thriving Children Advocates, alleges that Danish-Dutch investment fund Waterland and two Danish employees used confidential business information to build a competing sponsorship operation for Christian music tours. The allegations appear in a US lawsuit reviewed by DR; Waterland and the employees deny wrongdoing.

segments.title: A case still before the court
segments.body: The plaintiffs also allege that reporting about misconduct accusations against a Christian band’s former singer was used as part of a coordinated effort to harm their business. The defendants reject that account and say the suit lacks evidence of a conspiracy or harm to competition; they have asked a Tennessee judge to dismiss the case. The judge has yet to decide whether it will proceed.

content.headline: High electricity prices spur renewed interest in rooftop solar
content.shortHeadline: Rising power prices renew interest in household solar
content.standfirst: Solar installers report more enquiries and completed projects as electricity costs rise. Batteries can help households use daytime power later, while an energy researcher says rooftop generation could ease pressure on the grid if used where it is produced.

image.caption: Solar company director Kasper Bruhn says high electricity prices are bringing more customers.

sources.originalTitle: Solceller er populære: Vi gør det for pengepungens skyld
Er solceller for dig?

segments.body: Solar companies say demand for household panels has increased as electricity prices rise. One installer says more customers are moving from enquiries to completed installations. The Danish Solar Energy Association also reports renewed interest, following a similar surge when energy prices rose after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

segments.title: Savings depend on use
segments.body: A battery can store electricity generated during the day for use during morning or evening peaks, but a household’s savings depend on how much power it uses while the panels are producing. An independent adviser recommends comparing offers and considering roof replacement costs before investing; illustrative payback figures are not guarantees.

segments.title: Grid implications
segments.body: An energy researcher says electricity generated and consumed on the same building does not need to travel through the grid, which already faces limits on connecting new power. He estimates that suitable private rooftops could supply around 10–15% of expected Danish electricity use in 2030.

content.headline: Climate risk has yet to deter buyers of homes near Denmark’s coast
content.shortHeadline: Coastal home buyers still willing to take flood risk
content.standfirst: A family bought a plot near Kerteminde despite projections of future flooding, while preliminary research suggests climate risk may affect Danish property values less than some experts expect. Researchers say the work is not yet complete.

sources.originalTitle: Har købt sommerhusgrund i første række – i fremtiden risikerer den ikke længere at findes

segments.body: Niels Bækholm and his wife bought a summer-house plot close to the water at Langø, Kerteminde, despite a 2024 University of Southern Denmark report warning that flooding could threaten homes in the wider area by 2100. Bækholm says he understands the risk but values the project for the enjoyment it brings now.

segments.title: What the market may reflect
segments.body: The estate agent involved says local buyers ask more about flooding than before but remain willing to purchase. Curt Liliegreen of the Housing Economics Research Centre says preliminary analysis suggests climate threats may already affect prices, though perhaps not dramatically. He says a gradual fall could reduce future losses; the research is not complete and future prices remain uncertain.

content.headline: Skive’s royal-visit restaurant choice prompts union-agreement dispute
content.shortHeadline: Restaurant without a collective agreement chosen for royal visit
content.standfirst: Skive’s choice of a restaurant without a collective agreement for a royal-visit meal has drawn criticism from a local politician and 3F. The mayor says its location near a new waterfront facility made it the practical choice.

image.caption: King Frederik and Queen Mary are due to visit Skive for the town’s anniversary.

sources.originalTitle: Kongeparret er inviteret på restaurant uden overenskomst: Politiker kalder det forkert

segments.body: Skive Municipality plans to host King Frederik and Queen Mary at the Hereford Beefstouw restaurant during the town’s 700th-anniversary celebrations. Local SF politician Mie Johansen and the 3F union criticise the choice because the restaurant does not have a collective agreement.

segments.title: The municipality’s response
segments.body: Johansen says the municipality should set an example and choose a venue with an agreement, while stressing she is not making claims about the restaurant’s actual working conditions. Mayor Alfred Brunsgaard says the venue was chosen because it is near a waterfront facility the royal couple will open. He says the municipality cannot require a restaurant to have a collective agreement.

content.headline: Evans wins first WRC title after Solberg crashes in dramatic finale
content.shortHeadline: Evans claims first WRC title after Solberg crashes
content.standfirst: Elfyn Evans became Britain’s first world rally champion in 25 years after Oliver Solberg crashed near the end of the final stage in Sardinia. Evans finished the season five points clear.

image.caption: Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin, the 2026 World Rally Championship winners.

sources.originalTitle: Evans claims dramatic WRC title after Solberg crash

segments.body: Evans and co-driver Scott Martin entered the final round with a 21-point lead, but that had dwindled to one by the last of 17 stages. Solberg needed to beat his Toyota team-mate there to take the championship, but crashed with less than 100 metres remaining.

segments.title: A title decided at the finish
segments.body: Solberg recovered to win the rally, finishing ahead of nine-time world champion Sebastien Ogier, but the crash left him five points behind Evans in the season standings. Evans, a five-time runner-up, said he felt for Solberg and called his own title win surreal.

content.headline: England thrash Croatia 7-0 as Bellingham excels and Modric rues a 'catastrophic'
content.shortHeadline: England beat Croatia 7-0 as Bellingham shines
content.standfirst: England overwhelmed Croatia in the Nations League, with Jude Bellingham scoring and providing three assists. Luka Modric said he felt ashamed of Croatia’s performance after their heaviest defeat.

image.caption: Luka Modrić watches as Jude Bellingham congratulates Bukayo Saka during England’s 7-0 win over Croatia.

sources.originalTitle: Modric 'ashamed' of Croatia's 'catastrophic night'
Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest'

segments.body: England were 5-0 ahead when Modric was substituted in the 57th minute in Rijeka. Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka scored before Saka and Morgan Rogers added further goals. Modric called it a “catastrophic night” and said he had not felt ashamed after a match in his 20 years as an international.

segments.title: Bellingham’s performance
segments.body: Bellingham scored and assisted three goals, then wore the captain’s armband after Kane was rested. He became the first England player to record three assists in a match since Trent Alexander-Arnold in 2021.

perspectives.body: Roy Keane said Bellingham had the potential to become one of the greatest players of all time, praising his running, delivery and goal threat. Thomas Tuchel said the midfielder had reached another level but would need to keep developing.

content.headline: Wu Yize wins Shenzhen Open to claim first ranking title since world crown
content.shortHeadline: Wu wins Shenzhen Open after becoming world champion
content.standfirst: Wu Yize beat Yuan Sijun 10-5 in an all-Chinese final, claiming his first ranking title since winning the world championship. He rises to second in the rankings behind Zhao Xintong.

image.caption: Wu Yize’s victory at the Shenzhen Open was his third ranking title.

sources.originalTitle: Wu wins first title since Crucible at Shenzhen Open

segments.body: Wu took control in the evening session with breaks of 74 and 62 to move 8-5 ahead, then closed out the best-of-19 final. He had beaten Judd Trump 6-1 in the semi-finals; Yuan, playing his first ranking final, moves up seven places to 26th.
The 22-year-old’s win puts him second in the world rankings, ahead of Trump and Neil Robertson. China now has the top two players in the rankings for the first time.

content.headline: Bowie scores first Scotland goal in 2-0 win over North Macedonia
content.shortHeadline: Bowie opens Scotland account in 2-0 win
content.standfirst: Kieron Bowie scored his first Scotland goal as Sebastien Pocognoli’s side beat North Macedonia in Skopje, giving the new head coach his first win. Andy Robertson marked his 100th cap.

sources.originalTitle: Bowie seizing Scotland shot after World Cup disappointment
Scotland Men's Football Team

segments.body: Bowie struck in a 2-0 Nations League win, having missed out on Scotland’s World Cup squad and then had his first international start cut short against Switzerland. He said the new coach’s style suited his strengths and that he felt trusted.

segments.title: A milestone for Robertson
segments.body: Captain Andy Robertson earned his 100th Scotland cap in the win. He called the achievement special for him and his family, and said the team had defended well after a red card made the closing minutes difficult.

perspectives.body: Robertson apologised to team-mate Scott McKenna for the pass that preceded McKenna’s sending-off, while praising the side’s response and describing the result as a big win for the new manager.

content.headline: Djokovic rallies past Zverev to reach China Open semi-finals
content.shortHeadline: Djokovic beats Zverev to reach China Open semis
content.standfirst: Novak Djokovic came from a set down to beat world number two Alexander Zverev 4-6 6-4 6-4. He will face Daniil Medvedev for a place in the final as he pursues his first title of 2026.

image.caption: Novak Djokovic, who is seeking his first title of 2026.

sources.originalTitle: Djokovic beats Zverev to reach China Open semis

segments.body: After losing the first set, Djokovic broke Zverev at 5-4 in the second to level the match, then made the decisive break at the same score in the third. The win extended his unbeaten run in Beijing to 32 matches and moved him closer to a seventh China Open title.

content.headline: Bartunkova stuns Sabalenka as top two seeds exit China Open early
content.shortHeadline: Bartunkova shocks Sabalenka at China Open
content.standfirst: Nikola Bartunkova beat world number two Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 6-3, a day after top seed Elena Rybakina was knocked out. It is the first time since 2015 that the China Open’s top two seeds have both missed the last 16.

image.caption: Aryna Sabalenka was beaten by Nikola Bartunkova at the China Open.

sources.originalTitle: Sabalenka stunned by Bartunkova at China Open

segments.body: The 20-year-old Czech, ranked 34th, converted her opportunity against Sabalenka, who failed to take any of her five break points. Bartunkova said she focused on staying calm and was happy to beat a player she called a legend.

segments.title: An early exit for the top seeds
segments.body: Rybakina had been eliminated a day earlier by world number 118 Alina Charaeva. Sabalenka has not won a title since March’s Indian Wells and Miami tournaments; Rybakina later withdrew from the Wuhan Open, citing a foot injury.

content.headline: Marquez wins Japanese Grand Prix to close to two points behind Martin
content.shortHeadline: Marquez cuts Martin’s MotoGP lead to two points
content.standfirst: Marc Marquez won both the sprint and the race at Motegi, passing championship leader Jorge Martin on lap 11. Martin finished second, leaving him two points ahead with six rounds remaining.

image.caption: Marc Marquez, who won the Japanese Grand Prix and its sprint race.

sources.originalTitle: Marquez wins in Japan to cut Martin's MotoGP lead

segments.body: Martin started from pole and held the lead off the line, but Marquez moved past him on the inside on lap 11. Marquez said he waited for his chance and then increased his pace; Marco Bezzecchi finished third.

content.headline: Manchester City found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches
content.shortHeadline: Man City found guilty of Premier League financial breaches
content.standfirst: BBC Sport reports that Manchester City have been found guilty of charges relating to alleged breaches between 2009-10 and 2017-18. The supplied reports describe the scope of the findings differently and do not detail any sanctions.

sources.originalTitle: What have Man City been found guilty of doing?
What could the potential sanctions for Man City be?
Man City CEO refuses to answer questions on guilty verdict

segments.body: A BBC Sport explainer says City were found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules during the stated seasons. A separate explainer, citing sources, describes the finding as covering a “significant majority” of the 115 rules the club was accused of breaching.

segments.title: Response and possible sanctions
segments.body: City chief executive Ferran Soriano declined to answer BBC Sport’s questions about the charges at a conference of European clubs in Copenhagen. Football finance expert Kieran Maguire said potential sanctions would be “significant”; the supplied material does not specify what sanctions will be imposed.

perspectives.body: Soriano declined to answer questions from BBC Sport about the Premier League charges at the Copenhagen conference.

content.headline: Grouper’s Liz Harris finds wary hope in collaboration after a streaming scam
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris on collaboration, virality and scam artists
content.standfirst: A viral afterlife for an old song brought new listeners and a royalty scam; reforming dream-pop trio Helen, meanwhile, reminded the elusive artist of the restorative power of making music with friends.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Grouper and Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris has built Grouper’s intimate, elusive music while keeping the music industry at arm’s length. Then “Poison Tree,” a song she wrote in her twenties, took off online. Harris says someone had fraudulently registered and uploaded it, earning around six figures before she and her label shut down the scam and recovered what she was owed.

segments.title: A different kind of company
segments.body: The experience deepened Harris’s wariness of streaming platforms, where she says fake remixes and tracks with matching titles can be used to siphon royalties. But working again with her friends in Helen has offered a counterweight: the trio’s new album, Linda’s Head, brought her a welcome sense of shared purpose and, she says, was restorative during a difficult period.

content.headline: Erasure’s Andy Bell and Vince Clarke lean on four decades of friendship
content.shortHeadline: Erasure’s Andy Bell and Vince Clarke on friendship and grief
content.standfirst: Their 20th album arrives after a painful period for both bandmates, while Clarke steps away from touring following his wife’s death. Their conversation reveals the history and affection behind that decision.

image.caption: Vince Clarke and Andy Bell of Erasure.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring

segments.body: Andy Bell and Vince Clarke say their long friendship helped them through bereavement: Clarke’s wife, Tracy Hurley Martin, died in 2024, and Bell’s partner, Paul Hickey, died in 2012. Clarke credits Bell with giving him the support he needed. Their closeness also shapes the new Erasure album, Radio!! Radio!!, which Bell describes as a call for calmer times.

segments.title: A changed tour
segments.body: For the first time in Erasure’s history, Clarke will not perform on the band’s coming arena tour. He will serve remotely as musical director, with keyboard technician Howard Rider playing the parts on stage. Asked whether his wife’s death is the main reason, Clarke answers yes. Bell says the arrangement will not feel the same without his trusted partner beside him.

content.headline: Interpol’s new album brings fresh angles to the band’s familiar sound
content.shortHeadline: Interpol find new angles on This Mirror Weighs a Ton
content.standfirst: The band’s eighth album keeps its angular indie-rock identity but brings in new collaborators, a return to recording in New York and more varied arrangements. Its founders also challenge the rosy mythology of the early-2000s scene.

image.caption: Interpol founders Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler.

sources.originalTitle: Interpol: ‘People romanticise the Noughties music scene. We weren’t all friends’

segments.body: Interpol’s This Mirror Weighs a Ton is presented as a return to form, but the changes are part of the point. The band tried an outside producer, Andrew Wyatt, brought touring bassist Brad Truax into the writing process and recorded in New York for the first time since 2014. The result ranges from tense guitar-led songs to piano ballads and the band’s first use of acoustic guitar.

segments.title: A less romantic scene
segments.body: Founders Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler also push back on the idea that the early-2000s New York music scene was one big community of friends. They recall sharing clubs and a moment in time, but say the popular image of bands lending one another instruments and moving as a united circle did not match their experience.

content.headline: Venom’s Cronos brought punk’s unruly spirit to heavy metal
content.shortHeadline: Cronos made Venom’s metal raw, unruly and influential
content.standfirst: As frontman of Venom, Conrad “Cronos” Lant helped give black metal its name and pushed heavy music towards a rougher, more confrontational sound. His ferocious stage persona was only one part of a long career.

image.caption: Venom frontman Cronos performing in 1985.

sources.originalTitle: No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitude

segments.body: When Venom emerged from Newcastle in the late 1970s, Cronos thought metal had gone soft. The band answered with a DIY attack: hoarse vocals, hammering riffs and lyrics that made occult imagery deliberately confrontational. Venom’s 1982 album Black Metal gave a name to a subgenre, while Cronos’s snarling stage presence became a model for generations of metal frontmen.

segments.title: Beyond the stage persona
segments.body: The persona did not tell the whole story. Cronos left Venom for several years, trained as a fitness instructor and enjoyed birdwatching; he later returned to lead the band through more personnel changes. He also rejected the violence associated with some later black-metal acts, lamenting that they were known for it rather than their music.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond on Soft Cell’s final album and Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Marc Almond and Dave Ball had finished Danceteria together just two days before Ball died in 2025. Almond recalls their friendship and the New York nightlife that shaped the album’s bittersweet farewell.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell had agreed that their new songs were finished when Dave Ball died, two days later, in October 2025. For Marc Almond, that makes Danceteria the duo’s sixth and final album: he says he would not make another Soft Cell record without Ball. The album looks back to the pair’s early-1980s experiences in New York, both its exuberant clubs and its loneliness.

segments.title: A bond beyond the music
segments.body: Almond describes a friendship that survived nearly five decades without a serious falling-out. He is relieved they completed the record together, and remembers Ball as happy with it. Their recollections also follow the changing gay nightlife they knew: the freedom of the city’s underground clubs, followed by fear and loss as AIDS devastated the scene.

content.headline: Lulu returns to recording with new freedom after confronting addiction
content.shortHeadline: Lulu’s return to music comes with hard-won freedom
content.standfirst: The singer’s first new album in years is also a chance to set her own direction. She reflects on sobriety, the pressures that shaped her early career and the music that has repeatedly helped her begin again.

image.caption: Singer Lulu, whose new album marks a return to recording.

sources.originalTitle: Lulu: ‘I’m not proud of being an alcoholic – but I’m not ashamed’

segments.body: Lulu says writing about her past in her memoir was difficult but cathartic. She has spoken publicly about a long-hidden alcohol addiction and getting sober in 2013. “I’m not proud of it, but I’m not ashamed,” she says, describing the relief of no longer keeping that part of her life secret.

segments.title: A voice of her own
segments.body: Her new album, Let the Girl Sing Out, is being made with her brother Billy Lawrie, with Lulu co-writing and setting the artistic direction. She says that autonomy is what she wanted throughout a career in which others often steered her towards material that did not feel like her. Music, she says, has repeatedly opened a new beginning.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s debut comes into focus in a sprawling anniversary set
content.shortHeadline: A 104-track set reveals the making of Elvis Costello’s debut
content.standfirst: Pitchfork’s review finds the five-disc edition of My Aim Is True valuable not just as a trove for collectors, but as a portrait of a young songwriter gradually finding his voice and musical identity.

image.caption: Elvis Costello, whose debut album is revisited in a new anniversary edition.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The new 104-track edition follows Elvis Costello from earlier demos and recordings with Flip City to the songs and performances surrounding My Aim Is True. Pitchfork argues that the material makes the apparent leap of his debut feel less sudden: Costello was already a skilled songwriter, still trying out influences and approaches before punk-era urgency sharpened his persona.

segments.title: A complicated legacy
segments.body: The review sees the box set as a rare reissue that earns its scale. Demos and live recordings add context, while the finished album retains the wit, anger and tightly wound songwriting that made it a landmark. The later discs are less essential, but the collection’s arc gives fans a clearer view of how Declan MacManus became Elvis Costello.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul remains in motion in an expansive new edition
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul’s many versions come alive in a new box set
content.standfirst: The deluxe edition collects UK and US versions, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new remix. Pitchfork’s review argues that the album’s history is less a single definitive object than a record shaped by creative choices and commerce.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul marked a turning point for the Beatles and for pop, as the band joined self-written songs and adventurous arrangements to mass appeal. The new edition gathers its UK and US releases, mono and stereo mixes, outtakes and a new mix, letting listeners hear how recording decisions and the American track list produced different versions of the album.

segments.title: No single definitive version
segments.body: Pitchfork’s review finds the outtakes especially revealing: they show the band working quickly under pressure rather than simply fulfilling a story of inevitable greatness. Its central argument is that no one mix can settle the album’s meaning; each version brings a different balance of intimacy, punch and detail, and listeners arrive with their own preferred Rubber Soul.

content.headline: John Cena’s Hollywood career tests the limits of loyalty
content.shortHeadline: John Cena on Hollywood, WWE and the cost of loyalty
content.standfirst: The wrestler-turned-actor discusses his comic screen persona and his loyalty to WWE, including his continued friendship with former boss Vince McMahon, who denies allegations made in a former employee’s lawsuit.

image.caption: John Cena, wrestler and actor.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahon

segments.body: John Cena has moved from WWE stardom to a distinctive Hollywood career, often playing powerful men who are comfortable looking ridiculous. He describes his relationship with WWE as one of service and gratitude, and says the company has a legitimate share of ownership in the John Cena character he built there.

segments.title: An unresolved loyalty
segments.body: Cena says he feels no guilt or shame about his friendship with former WWE chairman Vince McMahon. McMahon resigned in 2024 after sexual-assault allegations and lawsuits, including a suit by former employee Janel Grant alleging assault and coercion. McMahon denies the allegations; the litigation was transferred to confidential private arbitration. Cena’s unwavering public support raises questions about the cost of his company loyalty.

content.headline: A Statement turns a failed climate meeting into absorbing human drama
content.shortHeadline: A Statement finds drama in a failed climate conference
content.standfirst: Tom McCarthy’s film draws much of its conference-room dialogue from the actual 1980 transcript, following experts as they struggle to agree on a response to climate change. Its ensemble drama makes the deadlock compelling without disguising the failure.

image.caption: A still from A Statement.

sources.originalTitle: A Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meeting

segments.body: In 1980, 20 experts met in Florida to advise Congress on climate change. A Statement recreates their marathon discussions, drawing the conference-room dialogue from the stenographer’s record. The group agreed on the underlying facts but never reached consensus or issued the requested statement.

segments.title: The people behind the debate
segments.body: The film’s strength, in the review’s view, is its ensemble: Paul Rudd moderates, Paul Giamatti brings wary pragmatism, and Evan Peters embodies urgency. The late-night conversations and personal reckonings beyond the official meeting give the historical debate emotional texture, while the failure to agree remains in plain sight.

content.headline: Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter concert film captures a singular night
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall is a concert film to savour
content.standfirst: Paul Thomas Anderson’s 35mm film preserves the spare performance and rapt audience that made Winter’s Carnegie Hall concert feel like a communion. It offers little to newcomers, but makes a striking document for listeners already drawn to his music.

image.caption: A still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.

sources.originalTitle: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic

segments.body: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall records the Geese frontman’s solo acoustic performance in a 75-minute film shot on 35mm. Paul Thomas Anderson was among the camera operators. The review praises the film’s rich colour and close attention to Winter’s voice, piano and the quiet of an audience focused on the music.

Anderson keeps the framing spare, largely letting the concert speak for itself. The result, the review argues, is a faithful record of a performance that felt less like a conventional show than a shared ritual. Its lack of interviews or explanatory material may limit its appeal beyond existing fans, but those who enter its world get a carefully made document of a defining night.

content.headline: After Blade stalled, Bassam Tariq and Mahershala Ali made a film of their own
content.shortHeadline: Bassam Tariq turned a stalled Blade project into a new film
content.standfirst: The director and Mahershala Ali brought ideas from the abandoned Marvel project into Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, a Houston-set thriller about faith, violence and fatherhood made on a more personal scale.

image.caption: Director Bassam Tariq at the Toronto Film Festival in September 2026.

sources.originalTitle: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’

segments.body: Bassam Tariq says the collapse of his planned Blade reboot left him and Mahershala Ali with action sequences and ideas they could redirect into Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother. Ali plays a devout Muslim father who works as a contract killer, while Jon Cho’s pastor character leads a rival religious crusade in Tariq’s pulpy Houston-set thriller.

segments.title: A personal starting point
segments.body: The film’s story began in part with Tariq’s own panic after his wife developed an infection following the birth of their child. He searched New York for breast milk for his son, an experience that fed the film’s opening crisis. Tariq says the story became a way to explore faith and the importance of being present as a father.

content.headline: Digger divides critics over Tom Cruise’s audacious oil-tycoon satire
content.shortHeadline: Digger splits critics on Cruise’s oil-tycoon performance
content.standfirst: Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s eco-satire gives Cruise an extreme transformation as an oil baron facing a climate catastrophe. One review calls it laborious and glib; another embraces its eccentric scale and political bluntness.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as oil tycoon Digger Rockwell in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: In Digger, Tom Cruise plays a paunchy Texas oil tycoon whose drilling operation helps trigger a global crisis. The Guardian review finds striking images in the film but calls its satire shallow and laborious, arguing that the plot’s major turn undercuts the drama and leaves the tycoon’s claims about energy policy insufficiently challenged.

perspectives.body: The BBC review also sees an eccentric, divisive film, but finds its high-concept turns and outsize performance purposeful. It praises the satire’s political force and argues that Cruise’s willingness to take such an odd role is evidence against a straightforward Oscar-bait reading.

segments.title: A risky change of register
segments.body: Both reviews note the scale of Cruise’s transformation and the distance from his familiar action roles. They disagree on whether the film’s excess becomes empty self-indulgence or an engaging experiment: the Guardian is unconvinced, while the BBC critic says the gargantuan performance and environmental argument won them over despite stretches that could have been shorter.

content.headline: James Dean’s fragile talent outlasts the myth of the rebel
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebel image
content.standfirst: A look back at East of Eden finds the actor’s most enduring quality not in his familiar image of cool defiance, but in a vulnerable performance shaped by his difficult relationship with his father and fear of fame.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean’s three starring roles made him an icon, but the profile argues that his performance in East of Eden is best understood through its vulnerability. Director Elia Kazan drew on Dean’s resentment towards his father when shaping Cal, the troubled son who cannot stop seeking his father’s approval.

segments.title: The moment that remains
segments.body: Dean died at 24, before the release of two of his star vehicles, and his death helped turn him into a symbol of living fast and dying young. The article returns instead to a scene in East of Eden where Cal embraces his father after his birthday gift is rejected: a raw, unscripted moment that reveals the desperate boy beneath the carefully preserved image.

content.headline: A new Sense and Sensibility makes Austen’s emotional balance feel current
content.shortHeadline: Sense and Sensibility still speaks to the social-media age
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker adaptation of Jane Austen’s novel is uneven, but its sisters’ competing instincts resonate with modern pressures around privacy, romance and financial security.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: The new film follows sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, whose contrasting responses to love and hardship give Jane Austen’s novel its title. The review finds Georgia Oakley’s adaptation uneven and gloomier than the 1995 film, but argues that the sisters’ struggle between restraint and romantic idealism remains recognisable.

segments.title: Heart, head and modern life
segments.body: The article connects Austen’s characters to a present-day tension: people are encouraged to share their feelings yet remain guarded in a world where private moments can be recorded and circulated. Marianne’s faith in a charming suitor obscures warning signs; Elinor’s restraint leaves her carrying grief alone. Austen’s question of how to live by feeling and judgement still travels.

content.headline: From Psycho to The Prestige: 15 films that land a great plot twist
content.shortHeadline: 15 film twists that still make audiences look twice
content.standfirst: This spoiler-aware guide revisits 15 memorable reversals, from Psycho’s early shock to later films that make viewers rethink the story they have been watching.

sources.originalTitle: The 15 best film plot twists of all time

segments.body: The list ranges across decades and genres, from Psycho and The Wicker Man to The Prestige, Parasite and M. Night Shyamalan’s The Sixth Sense. It foregrounds the turns themselves and how films use them to change the audience’s understanding of a character, a setting or the story’s rules.

The guide warns that spoilers are ahead. Its appeal is not simply the surprise, but the different ways a reveal can reframe what came before: a detective story becomes a character study, a family home turns uncanny, or a confident narrator proves unreliable.

content.headline: Friday Night Lights made small-town football a story about people
content.shortHeadline: Friday Night Lights found humanity beneath football’s glare
content.standfirst: Twenty years on, the drama’s handheld style, improvisational performances and close attention to Dillon, Texas, still distinguish it. Its football world is also one of pressure, inequality and hopes that do not always come true.

image.caption: Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different

segments.body: Friday Night Lights began with a high-school football town where a Friday game could shape the mood for days. The series drew on H.G. “Buzz” Bissinger’s reporting about Odessa, Texas, and carried forward its unease about racism, the pressure placed on young players and the resources football could draw away from schools.

segments.title: A different kind of realism
segments.body: Director Peter Berg encouraged improvisation and handheld camerawork, giving scenes a naturalism unusual for a network drama. Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton anchor the show as a coach and school counsellor trying to raise a family amid constant public scrutiny. Its five seasons also helped launch Jesse Plemons and Michael B. Jordan.

content.headline: Get Jiro turns food culture into a bloody satire of power
content.shortHeadline: Get Jiro serves food satire with a side of ultraviolence
content.standfirst: Anthony Bourdain’s graphic novel becomes an adult animation about chefs, crime and a future where food is the last pleasure that technology cannot virtualise. Its extravagant violence is part of a pointed joke about food’s status and power.

image.caption: Jiro, voiced by Brian Tee, in Get Jiro.

sources.originalTitle: Get Jiro: Anthony Bourdain’s ultraviolent sushi chef makes for wild, pulpy television

segments.body: In Get Jiro, food has become the last pleasure that a digital world cannot reproduce. In near-future Los Angeles, chefs wield the power of crime bosses and people will kill for restaurant reservations. The taciturn sushi chef Jiro is no innocent bystander: the opening scene makes clear how far the show will push its grotesque food jokes and violence.

The review finds the animation camp and knowingly excessive, with restaurant criticism and culinary jargon turned into street-level satire. Beneath the pulpy action, it sees an indictment of food as class currency, drawing on the graphic novel co-written by Anthony Bourdain, whose work joined kitchen machismo to empathy and curiosity about people.

content.headline: War turns a celebrity divorce into lavish, high-stakes television
content.shortHeadline: War makes a high-stakes game of divorce
content.standfirst: Sienna Miller and Dominic West lead George Kay’s glossy drama about a wealthy couple and the lawyers fighting over their separation. The review relishes its money, class conflict and escalating legal manoeuvres.

image.caption: James McArdle, Sienna Miller and Phoebe Fox in War.

sources.originalTitle: War review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive fun

segments.body: War centres on social-media mogul Morgan Henderson and actor Carla Duval, whose divorce becomes a public battle. Their legal teams—one established and old-fashioned, the other younger and more polished—look for leverage in their clients’ finances, reputations and relationships.

segments.title: Soap opera with legal briefs
segments.body: The review embraces the series as high-quality “balderdash”: a fast-moving tangle of prenups, betrayals, press tactics and double-crosses. Dominic West and Sienna Miller keep the central couple watchable without demanding sympathy, while Pip Torrens and a broad supporting cast give the legal shenanigans their own comic momentum.

content.headline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors blunder gives the celebrity series an early jolt
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors slip-up sets the series in motion
content.standfirst: The actor accidentally reveals his role almost as soon as he is chosen, creating a chaotic opening for the second celebrity series. The review argues that the misstep makes the game more compelling, not less.

image.caption: Richard E Grant and Maya Jama as the first hooded Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant

segments.body: After being chosen as a Traitor alongside Maya Jama, Richard E Grant tells Joe Lycett outright: “Oh, I’m a Traitor.” The review says the mistake was genuine, leaving Grant and Jama to manage the fallout while the Faithfuls try to work out why he would confess so quickly.

Rather than deflating the series, the blunder gives it a new source of suspense: Grant is delighted by the game, Jama tries to regain control, and the others are left guessing. The piece sees the show’s unpredictable personalities and high-camp atmosphere as the reason the format still feels fresh.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson brings a pleasure-first attitude to The Great British Bake Off
content.shortHeadline: Nigella brings pleasure, not guilt, to Bake Off
content.standfirst: The new judge’s delight in eating and refusal to call food “naughty” offer a welcome counterpoint to calorie-conscious food culture. A second review finds that her glamour also gives the familiar show a lift.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time
Nigella’s glamour saves Bake Off’s stale mix

segments.body: Nigella Lawson’s arrival as a Great British Bake Off judge has changed how the programme talks about food. She enjoys the bakes openly and objects when Paul Hollywood calls cookies “naughty”, saying people should take pleasure where they can. The review sees that response as a refreshing alternative to the pressure on women to monitor every bite.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s episode review also welcomes Lawson’s arrival, praising her confidence and sensual approach to baking as a boost to the familiar format. It notes that the show’s playful challenges remain, but argues her presence adds sophistication and star power.

segments.title: A different kind of judging
segments.body: Lawson’s approach contrasts with predecessor Prue Leith’s comments about whether a bake was worth the calories. The review argues that the contrast matters in a culture saturated with weight-loss messages: Bake Off becomes a mainstream space where a woman can enjoy rich food without apology or a calculation of how to compensate.

content.headline: Youth’s glamorous lead complicates its portrait of an ordinary middle-aged woman
content.shortHeadline: Youth asks who gets to look ordinary on television
content.standfirst: Sharon Horgan’s new comedy follows a 50-something woman juggling family, work and a changing body. The review praises the subject but questions whether a character framed as an everywoman can feel relatable when played by such a glamorous star.

image.caption: Sharon Horgan in Youth.

sources.originalTitle: Sharon Horgan’s Youth has one big problem

segments.body: Sharon Horgan created, wrote and stars in Youth as Alex, a literary agent dealing with a troubled teenage son, ageing parents, work pressures and changes to her body. The review sees value in a comedy about a woman in her fifties with a sex life, but argues that Horgan’s glamour can make the character feel remote from the “everywoman” the story intends.

segments.title: Who gets to be ordinary?
segments.body: The criticism is aimed less at Horgan than at television’s beauty standards. The piece argues that women are still expected to be exceptionally attractive to headline a show, even as stories give them more emotional complexity. It calls for the freedom to see women on screen as they are, rather than as an idealised version of themselves.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future looks uncertain, but fans still believe it can return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its latest pause
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership and cancelled a planned Christmas special, leaving the long-running series without a confirmed next chapter. Fans and writers disagree on why its recent revival faltered, but still want it back.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Peter Capaldi, Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since its latest series ended in 2025, Doctor Who has had no new episodes announced. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special; it is seeking another partner to help fund future production. The series also has no current Doctor, and the BBC has declined to discuss the decision.

segments.title: A format built to change
segments.body: The article traces the show’s repeated reinventions, from its 2005 revival to a succession of Doctors and showrunners. Fans and former writers offer different explanations for the latest decline, including scripts and the shape of the Disney+ partnership. They agree that regeneration and renewal have always been central to the show—and that an archive alone is not enough for its most devoted viewers.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a familiar legal drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up gives its legal drama a new British Asian family
content.standfirst: The spin-off moves the family-law format to Manchester and centres a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Its creators and stars discuss representation, family conflict and the freedom to build a new story.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, a barrister expected to take over her father’s Manchester law firm, until her mother’s death disrupts the succession plan. As in The Split, high-stakes divorce cases run alongside fractures within the lawyers’ own family. The new series has a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team.

segments.title: Normal lives on screen
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to create British Asian characters living ordinary lives rather than relying on familiar plots about terrorism or arranged marriage. Original-series creator Abi Morgan, now an executive producer, says the spin-off keeps the family drama’s emotional engine while giving a new writing team room to shape its own characters.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day’s excellent combat is trapped in repetitive design
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day has great combat and too little else
content.standfirst: The prequel makes firefights feel weighty and fluid, but repetitive routes, scattered collectibles and awkward exploration blunt the impact of its alien invasion story.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day returns to the day the Locust emerged from underground, putting players with Marcus Fenix and a squad of soldiers amid the invasion. The review praises the combat: characters move more naturally, cover feels better integrated and destructible environments make firefights vivid and tactical.

The surrounding campaign does not keep pace. The squad repeatedly crosses familiar areas, open levels are crowded with collectibles and side objectives, and exploring can trigger a mission failure. The review finds that the game’s strongest ideas arrive early, leaving its excellent combat to carry a safe and repetitive experience.

content.headline: Resident Evil’s new film recreates the fear of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil’s film finds horror in the experience of play
content.standfirst: Rather than centre familiar heroes, Zach Cregger’s adaptation follows an ordinary courier through the series’ escalating hazards, scarce ammunition and unsettling spaces. The result treats game mechanics as part of the horror.

image.caption: Zach Cregger on the set of the Resident Evil film.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil film does not feature familiar leads such as Leon or Claire. Instead, courier Bryan Hodukavich is caught in an outbreak with little equipment or understanding of what is happening. The film moves through recognisable game-like locations, from an abandoned farmhouse to a hospital and sewer, as Bryan finds weapons but remains short on ammunition.

The feature argues that Cregger adapts not just the franchise’s setting but the experience of play: moving through unfamiliar spaces, piecing together clues and never feeling certain of survival. It connects the film to other works that explore video-game rules and environments, rather than simply translating a game’s plot and heroes to the screen.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 makes the Top Gun fantasy feel unexpectedly moving
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 soars on thrilling dogfights and an engaging story
content.standfirst: The arcade flight game delivers spectacular combat and a more involving story than expected, though its crowded cockpit cues can confuse and its multiplayer was unavailable during review.

image.caption: A fighter jet in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 casts the player as a propaganda-invented ace pilot who becomes a real hero in the alternative world of Strangereal. Dogfights, bombing runs and unusual targets keep missions varied, while simplified and expert control options give newcomers and experienced pilots different ways into the action.

segments.title: An arcade game with feeling
segments.body: The review praises the game’s cinematic presentation, animated character scenes and orchestral score, saying the story lands more effectively than expected for an arcade flight sim. Visual clutter can make objectives hard to read, however, and the reviewer could not test online multiplayer because it was available only briefly during the review period.

content.headline: A free-Robux link can steal a child’s Roblox account
content.shortHeadline: How fake Roblox links trick children into losing Robux
content.standfirst: Scammers use lookalike sign-in pages to capture Roblox passwords and verification codes, then steal virtual currency or personal data. The safest step is to open the official app or site directly rather than follow a link.

image.caption: Roblox advises users to use its official app or website and avoid unfamiliar links.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: The scam begins with a promise of free Robux in a video comment or gaming chat. A link opens a fake login page that looks like Roblox; after entering their details, the child is redirected to the real site, which can make the theft hard to spot. Criminals may use or sell the stolen credentials and transfer a player’s currency.

segments.title: Keep login details private
segments.body: Cybersecurity experts advise children to open Roblox through its official app or website, not through links sent to them. Passwords, two-factor authentication codes and backup codes should never be shared. Roblox says it cannot guarantee that compromised accounts or lost currency can be restored, though it may recover items in limited circumstances.

content.headline: A father and son reconnect by replaying their old Call of Duty missions
content.shortHeadline: Replaying Call of Duty brings a father and son closer
content.standfirst: Returning to the co-op missions they first played when his son was five, a father finds that teamwork—and a few stubborn guard dogs—makes the old game feel new again.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game a father and son revisited together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: A father and his 22-year-old son revisit Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the first game they played together in co-op when the boy was five. They retry missions they never completed, discovering that their different approaches—one cautious, one charging ahead—still need to be reconciled.

They eventually work out how to play as a team and celebrate finishing a mission that defeated them years earlier. The essay becomes a reflection on the rare freedom of long gaming sessions in adulthood, and on a temporary stretch of time together before father and son move to different parts of the world.
